2545.t: Μost probably a derivation of Ἑλλοί (Helloí) or Σελλοί (Selloí), the Greek inhabitants of the area around the sanctuary of Dodona (Δωδώνη (Dōdṓnē)). The ultimate origin is unknown, possibly Pre-Greek.

2562.t: From φίλιππος (phílippos, “fond of horses”), from φιλέω (philéō, “to love”) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”).

2505.t: From Proto-Hellenic *trémō, from Proto-Indo-European *trem- (“to tremble”), extended form of Proto-Indo-European *ter-. The extended form Proto-Indo-European *tres- also yielded τρέω (tréō, “to dread, to terrify”).

2573.t: From δια- (dĭă-, “through”) + λογίζομαι (logĭ́zomai, “to count, reckon”), from λόγος (lógos, “word”) + -ίζω (-ĭ́zō).

2508.t: Perhaps from either Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰren- (“soul, mind; innards, diaphragm”), whence Old Norse grunr (“suspicion”), or *bʰren- (“front edge”), whence e.g.

2598.t: Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂k- (“to hit”), compare Latin lancea (“lance”) and Old Armenian գեղարդն (gełardn, “spear”), or a Semitic borrowing corresponding to Hebrew רֹמַח (rómaḥ, “spear”), Arabic رُمْح (rumḥ, “spear”) etc. (see the Arabic),…

2584.t: From καταρράσσω (katarrhā́ssō) + -της (-tēs), the former from κατα- (kata-, “down”) + ῥάσσω (rhā́ssō, “to strike, dash”).

2540.t: From ἐπιφανής (epĭphănḗs, “in view”) + -ια (-ĭă), from ἐπιφαίνω (epiphaínō, “to come into view”), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, bring to light”).

2565.t: From Proto-Hellenic *awistʰomai, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewis-dʰh₁-, from *h₂ew- (“to see, perceive”), from which also comes ἀΐω (aḯō).

2506.t: From Proto-Hellenic *témenos, from Proto-Indo-European *témh₁nos, from *temh₁- (“to cut”); whence τέμνω (témnō, “I cut”). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀳𐀕𐀜 (te-me-no).

2595.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ḱókʷ-ro-s, thematicized from *ḱókʷr̥ (“excrement”). Cognates include Old Irish cechar (“quagmire, slough, bog”), Sanskrit शकृत् (śakṛt, “dung”), and Lithuanian šiknà (“arse”), ši̇̀kti (“defecate”).

2549.t: From the reduplicated *si-sl̥h₂-sḱetor, from Proto-Indo-European *selh₂- (“mercy, comfort”). By surface analysis, ἵλαος (hī́laos, “propitious, gracious”) + -σκω (-skō).

2576.t: From διηγέομαι (dĭēgéomai, “set out in detail, describe”) + -σις (-sĭs).

2550.t: Related to ἵστημι (hĭ́stēmĭ), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”).

2511.t: From earlier *ἀϝάω (*ăwắō), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewh₂-, though without obvious cognates.

2556.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₃bʰel-, cognate with Old Armenian աւելի (aweli). Cf. ὀφείλω (opheílō).

2571.t: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“heaven, sky”), thus related to δῆλος (dêlos, “clear, visible”) and cognate to Latin dies

2539.t: ἐφίσταμαι [ἐπι-στα-] (ephístamai [epi-sta-], “stand on, over, or near”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agent noun suffix): literally, one who stands on, over, or near something or someone.

2569.t: From Proto-Indo-European *dwey- (“to fear”). Cognate with Ancient Greek δεινός (deinós), Latin dīrus, Old Armenian երկն (erkn).

2527.t: From ἐνδελεχέω (endelekhéō). Possibly related to latin Latin indulgeō, see there for more information.

2543.t: From ἐνδύω (endúō, “to clothe”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).

2589.t: Traditionally connected with κλάω (kláō, “to break”), but the semantics are tenuous, and there is no evidence for a long α (a) in the former. Thus, Beekes suggests a Pre-Greek origin.

2592.t: A technical loan of unknown origin. Walde suggested a connection with Proto-Germanic *hlaibaz (“loaf”), while Lewy proposed a Semitic origin; both proposals are unconvincing.

2507.t: From Proto-Indo-European *téh₁. Cognate with Gothic 𐌸𐌴 (þē).

2510.t: Traditionally compared to Sanskrit प्साति (psā́ti, “to eat, consume”).

2530.t: From ἐν- (en-, “in”) + τυγχάνω (tunkhánō, “to happen (to), I succeed, I light upon, I obtain”).

2599.t: From λυτρόω (lutróō, “to ransom”) + -σις (-sis, “a suffix added to verb stems to form abstract nouns or nouns of action, result or process”)

2533.t: From ἐξ- (ex-, “ex-, from”) + ἐτάζω (etázō, “to examine, test”).

2500.t: From συν- (sŭn-) + σκότος (skótos, “darkness”) + -άζω (-ắzō); the unprefixed verb σκοτάζω (skotắzō) is attested later.

2597.t: Likely from λᾶς (lâs, contracted form of λᾶας (lâăs, “stone”)) + *ξεύω (*xeúō, unattested variant of ξέω (xéō, “to smooth; to polish”)).

2536.t: From ἐπι- (epi-) + ἀγγέλλω (angéllō). (to promise): Compare typologically Latin prōmittō (< Latin mittō); Russian сули́ть (sulítʹ) (? akin to слать (slatʹ)).

2593.t: By surface analysis, κρότος (krótos) + -έω (-éō). Probably from Proto-Hellenic *krotéō, from Proto-Indo-European *krotéyeti, a causative verb from the root *kret- (“to rattle”).
